solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Vegetable container holding some Swedes one removed

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece sits within the other
something removed is taken away, so a letter is dropped from the group

blocks.note: a cage is a container for an animal
ABBA were a Swedish pop group, so some Swedes
A means one, as in a single thing; it is the letter taken out

explanation.surface: A crate of vegetables has had one of its swedes, the root vegetable, taken out.
explanation.walkthrough: Swedes look like root vegetables beside 'Vegetable', but here they are people from Sweden, the pop group. 'One' is the article A, removed before the group goes into the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A cabbage is a leafy green garden crop, one of the commonest examples of the category.

clue.text: The King’s taking a taxi?

indicators.note: to take something in is to receive it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: CR stands for Carolus Rex, Latin for King Charles
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monarch hails a cab instead of using the royal carriage.
explanation.walkthrough: CR is the royal cipher of a King Charles (Carolus Rex). The question mark admits that a taxi is just one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxi is one kind of motor vehicle hired for journeys, hence an example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Cents regularly covered by dollars — lots of them

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
something covered by another is enclosed in it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: bucks is American slang for dollars
the second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Small change hidden under piles of banknotes, and plenty of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads with its object: you can have buckets of them, meaning lots of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, buckets means a very large amount, as in rain falling in buckets or crying buckets.

clue.text: Part of orchard with pear peel scattered around the bottom of it

indicators.note: scattered things are strewn about in no order, so the letters are rearranged
the bottom of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
the final letter of the small word

explanation.surface: Somewhere in an orchard, pear peelings lie strewn around the foot of a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of PEAR PEEL plus the T at the end of 'it' rearrange into APPLE TREE.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchard is a planting of fruit trees, so a single fruit tree makes up one part of it.

clue.text: My relative to marry English politician, tackily, on vacation

definitions.note: a cryptic definition: emptying MARRY of its inside letters leaves MY

indicators.note: a vacated building has nobody inside, so only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
Member of Parliament
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Someone's relative marries a British MP in a gaudy wedding while the family is off on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a joke: take the middle out of MARRY and MY is what remains, so MY is the hollowed-out version of MARRY. 'My relative' looks like a family member but means the word My.
explanation.definitionFit: Removing the inner letters of one word to leave another is exactly what emptying that word does in crossword terms.

clue.text: Wings from peregrine and a cuckoo make a tasty snack

indicators.note: the wings of a bird are its two sides, so the outer letters are taken

blocks.note: first and last letters of the falcon's name
taken as written
cuckoo and nuts both mean crazy

explanation.surface: Parts of a falcon and a cuckoo end up as a bird-based snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Both birds are red herrings: 'peregrine' supplies only its outside letters and 'cuckoo' is an adjective meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Peanuts are a salted nibble often served with drinks, a typical bar snack.

clue.text: Bird in twisted net free, say, to rise

indicators.note: something twisted round is turned the other way, so the word is read backwards
in a down clue rising means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a net is a trap for catching things
to free of something is to rid of it
say means for example, e.g.

explanation.surface: A bird caught in a tangled net is released and flies up.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate reversals: 'twisted' turns the net, and 'to rise' turns the abbreviation for 'say', since a down answer read upwards runs backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The partridge is a plump game bird of fields and hedgerows, so it is a member of the class.

clue.text: A sailor from the south who’s a big strapping lad

indicators.note: in a down answer, reading from the south means starting at the bottom, so the word runs upwards

blocks.note: taken as written
an old salt is an experienced sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor from the southern hemisphere who is a well-built young man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the south' sounds like where the sailor comes from, but it tells you to read SALT upwards in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Atlas was the Titan who held up the heavens, so his name stands for any musclebound strongman.

clue.text: Metal skull about to be replaced by you

indicators.note: replacing one thing with another swaps them, so a letter is exchanged for a new one

blocks.note: the cranium is the skull
c (circa) means about; it is the letter swapped out
text-speak spelling, the letter that sounds like the word

explanation.surface: A metal plate fitted into a damaged skull, with your own bone taken out.
explanation.walkthrough: C stands for circa, Latin for about. Swap the C of CRANIUM for U and you have URANIUM.
explanation.definitionFit: Uranium is a heavy radioactive element classed among the metals, used as nuclear fuel.

clue.text: Yellowhammers originally found in tangled treetops, empty eaves and pigeonholes

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so the first letter is taken
tangled things are knotted out of order, so the letters are rearranged
an emptied word has lost its contents, so only its outer letters remain

blocks.note: the opening letter of the bird's name
taken as written, as letters to rearrange
first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Yellowhammers, a kind of songbird, are nesting in messy treetops, empty eaves and the holes of a dovecote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pigeonholes' fits the bird picture as nest holes, but it is a verb meaning categorises. The selected letters join the tangled word before the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: To pigeonhole people is to file them into fixed categories, which is what labelling them by cliché does.

clue.text: I see crowds prepare strange edible substance

indicators.note: to crowd something is to press in all round it, so one piece surrounds another
something strange is out of its normal form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
I plus C, the letter that sounds like see

explanation.surface: A cook notices a crowd gathering to make an odd foodstuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I see' sounds like a remark, but it spells I plus the letter C; the rearranged letters press in around that pair after their first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Rice paper is a thin translucent sheet that can be eaten, used for spring rolls and under macaroons.

clue.text: Set out from the Champs-Elysees?

blocks.note: the French word for the, prompted by the Paris setting
the Champs-Elysees is a famous Paris avenue, abbreviated AVE

explanation.surface: Starting a journey from the most famous boulevard in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'the Champs-Elysees' is read as a French-English phrase: le (the) plus AVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To set out is to depart on a journey, which is exactly what going away from a place means.

clue.text: ‘Flying V’ guitar engineered, electrified and strung, initially, by European

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so the first letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: opening letters of the four words, skipping 'and'
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A Flying V, the famous Gibson electric guitar shape, built and strung by a European maker.
explanation.walkthrough: The Flying V is a real electric guitar, which drives the whole surface, but here it describes birds flying in a V formation.
explanation.definitionFit: Migrating geese travel in a V-shaped skein, so a flying V is a cryptic picture of them.

clue.text: What makes a man? Being treated with regard?

indicators.note: something treated has been processed or worked on, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A philosophical question: is it respect from others that makes someone a man?
explanation.walkthrough: The question sounds like one about manhood, but the man in mind is the biscuit figure of the fairy tale.
explanation.definitionFit: A gingerbread man is a spiced biscuit cut into a human shape, so this dough is what such a man is made of.

clue.text: County court fool with one about to leave on large horse

indicators.note: whatever leaves is no longer there, so letters are dropped

blocks.note: Yorick was the king's jester whose skull Hamlet holds
I is the Roman numeral one; it drops out
c (circa) means about; it drops out too
a shire is a big English draught horse

explanation.surface: A county court jester rides about on a big horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'County court' reads as one legal phrase, but County is the definition and 'court fool' is Shakespeare's YORICK, who loses I and C.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkshire is the largest historic county of northern England, so it is an instance of one.

clue.text: Scheme to turn on Mother Teresa, perhaps with alcohol

indicators.note: turning something round faces it the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written before being turned
Mother Teresa was canonised, so she is an example of a saint, ST
rum is a kind of alcohol

explanation.surface: A plot to turn against Mother Teresa, fuelled by drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks Mother Teresa as an example of a saint, giving ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a pet remedy or favourite plan for solving a problem, often a dubious one.

clue.text: Baby of popular crossword setter with sensible clothing

indicators.note: here with means wearing, so one piece is dressed in the other

blocks.note: in means fashionable or popular
the setter refers to themselves as I
mature means sensible; it clothes the other pieces

explanation.surface: The baby of a well-loved crossword setter is dressed in practical clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baby' looks like a noun but works as an adjective meaning very small, as in baby carrots. MATURE wears IN and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Something miniature is a small-scale version, just as baby vegetables are tiny ones.

clue.text: Holding wheel, Mr Toad snarls: ‘Step on it!’

indicators.note: holding something keeps it within, so one piece is put inside
a snarl is a tangle, so the letters are knotted into a new order

blocks.note: a wheel is round, like the letter O
taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Mr Toad of The Wind in the Willows, gripping the steering wheel, yells at someone to drive faster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step on it!' is a driver's cry to accelerate, but read literally it is an invitation to tread on the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A doormat is the mat at a doorway that visitors walk on to wipe their shoes, so it exists to be trodden on.

clue.text: Romeo’s left depressed, finally, because drugged-up Juliet woke too late

indicators.note: in a down answer, pushing something down sends it to the bottom, so the L moves from top to end
finally means at the end, so the last letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: Romeo is a lover, and the 's adds the S
closing letters of the three words

explanation.surface: Romeo dies in despair because Juliet, drugged by the friar's potion, wakes up too late: the end of the play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' is the abbreviation L, and 'depressed' pushes it down to the bottom of LOVER'S in this down answer, giving OVERSL.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversleep is to stay asleep beyond the intended time, so it means waking later than planned.

clue.text: Exotic sea bird from China?

indicators.note: something exotic is unfamiliar and strange, so the letters take an unusual form

blocks.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A strange seabird that has come from China.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows that China is just one example of a place in the East.
explanation.definitionFit: China lies in East Asia, so something from there is described as oriental, an example of the broader sense.

clue.text: One piercing terrible abscess scratching bottom, resulting in infection

indicators.note: to pierce is to go into, so one piece is stuck inside the other
something terrible is in a bad state, so the letters are mangled
scratching out means erasing, so the final letter is struck off

blocks.note: the word without its last letter, ready to rearrange
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Picking at a nasty abscess on your bottom gives you an infection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratching' fits the itchy picture, but here it means crossing out the end of ABSCESS. I then goes into the rearranged SCABES.
explanation.definitionFit: Scabies is a contagious skin disease caused by burrowing mites, a parasitic infestation of the skin.

clue.text: Tear clothing from emissary accompanying cycling Spaniard

indicators.note: clothing covers the outside, so only the outer letters are taken
cycling goes round and round, so a letter moves from one end to the other

blocks.note: first and last letters only
Pedro is a typical Spanish man's name

explanation.surface: Ripping the clothes off an envoy who is riding alongside a Spanish cyclist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' looks like the verb to rip, but it is the noun for a drop of water from the eye. Cycling PEDRO sends the P to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A tear is a single bead of salty liquid falling from the eye when someone cries.

clue.text: Turn about car getting tailed on the southern edge of Baltimore

indicators.note: tailing something cuts off its end, as with tailing vegetables, so the last letter goes
in a word written across, its southern edge is taken here as the final letter

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
a Volvo is a make of car; it loses its last letter
the closing letter of the city's name

explanation.surface: A car pulls a U-turn while being followed on the southern outskirts of Baltimore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailed' suggests being followed by police, but it means docked of its tail. In this down answer the E sits at the bottom, the southern end.
explanation.definitionFit: To revolve is to rotate around an axis, so it is a direct synonym of the verb meaning rotate.

clue.text: Plant delivering Stairway to Heaven?

blocks.note: surface reading: a record plant pressing copies of the Led Zeppelin song, or Robert Plant, its singer, performing it
setter's reading: a growing plant that gave Jack a ladder up to the giant's castle in the clouds

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Plant sang Led Zeppelin's Stairway to Heaven, so the clue reads like rock trivia; it means the fairy-tale plant Jack climbed to the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jack and the Beanstalk, a magic plant grows from beans up into the clouds, giving a route to a land in the sky.

clue.text: Musical instrument made by Roland is getting set up

indicators.note: in a down answer, setting something up raises it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: Roland Rat was a puppet rat on 1980s British breakfast television
taken as written

explanation.surface: A musical instrument built by Roland, the electronic keyboard maker, is being assembled.
explanation.walkthrough: Roland is a real maker of synthesisers, but here Roland is the TV puppet Roland Rat, giving RAT.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitar is a long-necked plucked string instrument from India, so it is a member of the class.

clue.text: Piece of cake BA Baracus eats

definitions.note: eats is a plural slang noun for food; a kebab is one item of it

indicators.note: a piece is only part of a whole, so the letters lie within a longer run

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the end of one word, the middle one and the start of the last

explanation.surface: B.A. Baracus, the tough guy of The A-Team, eats something easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' reads as a phrase for an easy job, and 'eats' as a verb; in fact 'eats' is a noun for food. B.A. Baracus was Mr T's character in The A-Team.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is casual slang for food, and a kebab is a typical takeaway meal of grilled meat.

clue.text: Banks stops the shot

blocks.note: first meaning: puts money away in an account
second meaning: what a goalkeeper does when blocking an attempt on goal

explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Banks was England's 1966 World Cup goalkeeper, so the clue reads as him making a stop; Banks is really the verb for putting money aside.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to keep money for later and, in football, to stop a shot from going into the goal.

clue.text: Are old ones beginning to tire?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
I is one, so more than one is IS
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Are elderly people starting to get tired?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' looks like the start of a question but is the definition, the plural of the verb to be.
explanation.definitionFit: To be, in its sense of having reality, means to live or have being, so they are means they live on.

clue.text: Rain covers Mr Kelly, exposed, holding black article in America

indicators.note: something exposed has had its covering stripped, so the outer letters are removed
holding something keeps it within, so one piece is put inside
in places pieces inside another

blocks.note: the United States
taken as written
abbreviation used on pencils
the word with its first and last letters removed
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Gene Kelly, star of Singin' in the Rain, caught in the open in a downpour in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Gene Kelly danced with an umbrella in Singin' in the Rain, which makes the surface apt. The whole string of pieces sits inside the American abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbrella is a folding canopy that shields a person from rainfall, so these are coverings against wet weather.

clue.text: Warm to a detached farm property

indicators.note: detaching something separates it off, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: toasty means pleasantly warm
taken as written; these letters come away

explanation.surface: An estate agent's advert for a cosy detached house on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detached' sounds like estate-agent jargon for a house standing alone, but it is the instruction to pull TO A off TOASTY.
explanation.definitionFit: A sty is the pen where pigs are kept, one of the buildings a farm would own.

clue.text: Earn pennies before fleeced men start to rally

indicators.note: a fleeced sheep has had its outer coat sheared away, so only the inside is left

blocks.note: d was the abbreviation for old British pennies, from the Latin denarius
the word stripped of its outside letters
a rally in tennis begins with a serve

explanation.surface: Swindled workers earn a few pennies before a protest begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rally' suggests a political gathering, but it is a tennis rally, which starts with a serve.
explanation.definitionFit: To deserve something is to have merited or warranted it through effort, the sense of earning a reward.

clue.text: Mad tradesman loses face before going around and beating people up

indicators.note: the face is the front, so losing it drops the first letter
going around something encircles it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland, a hat-maker by trade
by means before, as in by noon

explanation.surface: A crazed shopkeeper, humiliated, goes on a violent rampage.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mad Hatter is the hat-maker from Alice in Wonderland. 'Before' looks like a word of order but is itself a piece, meaning by, as in by noon.
explanation.definitionFit: Battery is the legal term for the crime of physically attacking someone, so assault and beating.
